Season Guide

Each row runs January through December. Brighter cells mean a better bite; black cells are months closed to harvest — a season that turns over mid-month blacks out the whole month, so check the exact dates before you keep a fish. General patterns for the Ponce de Leon Inlet region, not a fishing report.

Recreational limits for Atlantic waters off Volusia County. Size is inches (") of total length unless the row says fork. Bag Limit is fish per person per day unless the row says otherwise. Each row says where its limits apply — Inside 3 mi is Florida state water, the dashed line on the map; Inside & beyond 3 mi means the same limits hold in federal water too. Tap a row’s FWC ↗ for FWC’s page on that fish (needs a signal). Use the Fish Rules App (fishrulesapp.com) to identify fish and confirm current state and federal rules.

Season bars and regulations are for the Northeast zone — north of the NSB South Causeway. South of it, in the Indian River Lagoon zone including Mosquito Lagoon, redfish, seatrout and a few others differ; each row’s note says how.

A bag limit is also a possession limit — the most you may have aboard at any one time, however many days you have been out. Limits are per person unless the row names a vessel limit, which caps the whole boat. Do not keep a fish for someone who is not fishing. Keep fish whole — head and tail attached — until you are ashore, so they can be measured.

⚠ Internet is required to update the app for the current FWC regulations. (Last updated —.) Limits refresh on their own whenever you open the app with a signal — no download — and REGULATION CHANGES below lists what moved. Offline you keep the last set your phone saw. Trust But Verify! 🔍

Every catch you log shows up here and as a diamond marker on the map, colored by species. Entries are listed by date caught, most recent first — not by the order you added them. Use EDIT ✎ to edit an entry or DELETE ✕ to delete it — UNDO below reverses your most recent change, one change per tap. Scroll to the bottom of your log to see the two ways to export/import your log.

Recently deleted: none.

Full backup — everything, photos included

Your catch log with its photos, your spot notes, the spots and launches you added yourself, any edits or deletions you made to built-in spots, and your drop labels. This is the file to keep. Photos make it large — often tens of megabytes — so it usually will not go through email. Use Share → AirDrop, Save to Files, or iCloud Drive.

Log only — no photos, small enough to email

The same catch log, notes, your own spots, spot edits and drop labels — with every photo left out. Usually a few kilobytes, so it attaches to mail or a text message without complaint. Imported catches come in with no photo attached, and nothing can put those photos back later.

Import

Reads either file back in — on this device, another one, or a fresh copy of the app. Nothing is overwritten: existing catches, notes, spots and labels are left alone and only items this device has never seen are added.

⚠ What each file does and doesn't carry. Photos live only inside the full backup; the log-only file drops them on purpose and they cannot be recovered from it. Your catch log — species, date, time, tide, position, notes — is complete in both. Spots are in both as well: the ones you added, the built-in ones you renamed, moved or deleted, and the names you gave individual reef drops. Everything lives on this device only — clearing the browser's website data, or deleting the app from your home screen, takes it with it. Export something before you change phones.

Read This Paragraph to Get Hooked

Tap any pin on the map for that spot's coordinates and details. + Catch logs a fish — one species or several — where you caught it and details. + Spot saves your position or any place you tap on the map, with details and season bars for the fish you name. Bite shows 3-day feeding times. With Tides selected, tap anywhere on the water for a 3-day tide forecast. Waves provide NOAA's offshore buoy data. My Log shows all your catches' info. Seasons show feeding times by month and fishing regs. Tap Compass and one or more offshore pins to get bearings and distance. Topo Satellite → Hi Res & ICW → Street Map. A short tap on Locate Me puts a pin at your location, but a 1-second press on the button triggers the MOB (man-overboard) function. Tap any Species button to filter your total number of catches. Everything is kept on your device. Read further to learn how to add your own tide station, download the offline map so it works without Internet, and back up all your photos and data. Not for navigation.

Get out there and have some REEL FUN! 🎣

Prints this entire help as plain text — every button’s writeup opened out — so it can be read offline or carried on paper.

Every part of this help sits behind a button. Tap a button to read it, and close it again either by tapping its title or with the CLOSE ✕ button at the end of the writeup. If you tap CLOSE ✕ at the top to exit Help and then return, Help will reopen to your last button view.

Action Buttons

Ten buttons along the right side of the map are the app’s actions. Tap any button below to read what it does and tap again to close.

Catch opens the log-a-catch form. Tap + Catch and pick the species from the list — tap more than one if the trip produced several; the first you tap colors the catch pin on the map, and every one you pick shows its season bar on the entry's My Log card and popup. Set date and time (shown in local 12-hour time), then set the location three ways: choose a known spot from the alphabetical list for Inshore or Offshore, Drop a pin on map, or Use my location. Clear removes a dropped pin. Next pick the tide by hand (High, Low, Falling, or Rising) or tap Auto-detect from NOAA once a location and date/time are set — the app looks up the nearest NOAA tide station's predictions for that exact moment (works for past dates too; but needs internet). The Location list includes every baked-in fishing spot — inshore and offshore, plus any spot you've added yourself. Boat ramps and kayak launches are left out, because they're land points rather than places you fish; but use Drop pin or My location if you did catch something close by one. The Inshore and Offshore pills just above the location list narrow it down to where you are fishing: they start black with the whole list showing, and tapping Offshore lights it purple and cuts the list to offshore sites only (Inshore does the same in blue). Tapping the lit one again turns it black and brings the whole list back. Size takes Length as ft and inches and Weight as lb and ounces — numbers only, and either box of a pair works alone (30 inches records the same fish as 2 ft 6 in).

Entering the GPS position. All coordinates display in degrees and decimal minutes (e.g. 29°04.902′ N) — the form a chartplotter uses. A catch takes its position three ways: pick a known spot from the location list, Drop a pin on map, or Use my location. The line under those buttons prints the position it settled on, so you can check it before saving, and Clear starts over. A photo with embedded GPS fills the position in by itself (see the photo note below). To key or paste numbers in by hand, save them in + Spot first — its position box reads typed and pasted coordinates in every common form — and the new spot is then in this location list.

+ Catch allows you to store a photo from your gallery — photos are stored on your device at high quality. If the photo has embedded GPS and a timestamp, the app fills in the catch location, date, and time automatically, and looks up the tide for that moment from NOAA. If it doesn't (photos sent through messaging apps usually lose this data), simply set the date and location yourself, then tap the tide buttons or NOAA auto-detect — everything stays editable before you save. Photos need to be in a format your browser can open — JPEG always works. Safari can read iPhone HEIC files, but Chrome, Edge and Firefox can't; if a photo is refused, set Settings → Camera → Formats → Most Compatible on your iPhone so new photos save as JPEG.

Edit or delete a catch: tap a catch diamond on the map and use EDIT ✎ or DELETE ✕ in its popup — or the same buttons on any entry in the My Log sheet. Editing reopens the form with everything filled in.

Spot saves your fishing location on the map. It's only stored on your device and shows up like the built-in spots, including in the + Catch location list. Drop a pin or use your current location and name it. A Details box takes anything worth remembering — structure, bait, tide — and if you name the fish you catch there (redfish, trout, snook, any species the app knows, by common nicknames too), the spot gets their season bars: on its pin's popup and beside its entry under Your saved spots. Every catch shows its species' season bar too, in its pin popup and on its My Log card. You can add and delete both fishing spots and launches, and the same goes for the ones that came with the app: tap any pin and use EDIT ✎ to rename or move it, or DELETE ✕ to take it off the map. The Inshore, Offshore and Launches totals in the map filter buttons at the top update the moment you add or delete one, either way. Deleting a built-in spot only hides it on this device — ↺ Restore built-in spots in the Add-a-spot sheet brings every one of them back. Deleted the wrong thing? UNDO above Your saved spots (or at the top of My Log) steps back through your last 10 changes, one per tap — and a deleted catch or spot stays restorable for 14 days (the last 10 deletions), even after the app is closed. Your own spots, your edits to built-in ones, and your drop labels all travel in either backup file. Cleared MOB marks land in this same list — red pins named MOB with their date and time — and are deleted the same way, with DELETE ✕ beside the entry under Your saved spots.

The type sets itself. You no longer have to pick inshore, offshore or launch before you save — drop the pin and the app reads the position and lights the matching pill. It works in three steps. If the pin lands within a couple of hundred yards of a spot that is already on the map, it takes that spot's type, so a pin at a known ramp comes up Launch and a pin on a known reef comes up Offshore. Failing that, if the pin is east of the beach it is Offshore. Failing that, if it sits on one of the waterways the app already follows for tide timing — the Halifax, the Indian River and the lagoon, Spruce Creek, Rose Bay, Turnbull Bay — it is Inshore. Anything left over is inland but off the water, which is what a ramp or a bank access looks like, so it comes up Launch. The line under the pills always says which of those decided it.

Check it before you save. The app carries a coarse beach line and channel centrelines, not a real shoreline, so the water's edge is the one place the guess goes wrong: a ramp right at the water can read Inshore, and a spot a few hundred yards up a narrow creek can read Launch. Every guess is only a suggestion — tap the right pill and your choice is what gets saved. Your own corrections also feed the first step above, so a ramp you save yourself will be recognised the next time you drop a pin near it. Exactly one pill is ever lit; the other two sit black and dimmed.

Typing or pasting a position. All coordinates display in degrees and decimal minutes (e.g. 29°04.902′ N) but can be entered several ways. Anywhere the app asks for a position — here in Add a Spot, and in Add a tide gauge — you can type or paste a coordinate straight into the box. Pasting works normally: copy the numbers off a chartplotter screenshot, an email or a text message, drop them in, and the preview under the box updates as you go. It reads the pair as you write it, so nothing has to be converted first.

Degrees and decimal minutes (DM) is what the app itself uses everywhere, and it is the form to prefer: 29 04.902 N, 80 56.202 W. The degree and minute marks are optional — 29°04.902′ N 80°56.202′ W reads the same. Commas, extra spaces, and the hemisphere letter before or after the number are all fine.

About the minus sign in DM: you do not need one if you write the N/S/E/W letter, and the letter always wins. If you leave the letters off, put the minus on the degrees only, never on the minutes — 29 04.902 -80 56.202 is correct, and every position in this area has a negative longitude because it is west. Writing -80 -56.202 is wrong and will land the pin in the wrong place.

Other forms that work. Full degrees, minutes and seconds (DMS): 29°04′54″N 80°56′12″W, or plainly as 29 4 54 N 80 56 12 W — the same minus-sign rule applies, degrees only. Decimal degrees: 29.0817 -80.9367. And the run-together plotter form 29.04.902 N, with two dots, is read as degrees and decimal minutes, not as a decimal degree.

If you type numbers with no hemisphere letters at all, give exactly two, four or six of them — two for decimal degrees, four for DM, six for DMS. Anything else is ambiguous and the box will say it could not read it. Latitude always comes first unless an E or W letter says otherwise.

Tap any pin, then tap ＋ Add my note at the bottom of its popup. Type your details — bait, rig, tide, timing — and Save. Notes persist between sessions and can be edited or cleared anytime with ✎ Edit my note.

Bite opens a 3-day solunar feeding forecast — the moon phase and % lit at the top, then Major and Minor feeding windows for that day, in the order they occur. Majors center on the moon overhead or underfoot; minors center on moonrise and moonset. Computed fully offline from moon-position astronomy, no internet is needed.

Tides let you tap anywhere on the map to drop a Tide pin — you get a 3-day high/low forecast, built from official NOAA predictions for Ponce Inlet stored on your device (currently through July 2027). Instead of just borrowing the nearest station's timing, the app measures how far your pin sits along the same waterway and interpolates the tide lag by distance between the calibrated stations on that arm — or extrapolates past the last one when you're farther upstream. Each forecast carries a confidence badge: High when you're on or between calibrated stations, and Low (with a ⚠) when the timing is extrapolated, off the mapped channel, or in a shallow wind-driven reach. Again, no internet is needed. Tides also brings the tide gauge pins up. They are the marks your forecast is timed from, so they show while Tides is lit — from the tap that arms the pin, through the forecast panel — and come off the chart when it goes out. The button turns the whole job off in one tap: the panel closes, the dropped pin goes, and the gauges go with them.

The tide gauges show on the map as black and gold pins with three wavey lines and an up/down arrow beside them, and they are only up while Tides is lit — they are working marks for reading a forecast against, not chart furniture, so they stay off until you are asking about the tide. Tap one to read its offset (lag times). Heights are scaled as well as times: the tide swings about 2.7 ft at Ponce Inlet but only half a foot at Ormond and five inches at Turtle Mound, so the app shrinks the inlet's heights to match the water you're actually on. Each waterway has its own zero-lag reference, and the app carries a full year of official NOAA predictions for both. Ponce Inlet anchors everything north up the Halifax; Ponce De Leon Inlet South, just inside the inlet, anchors the Indian River North and the lagoon. Every other gauge is timed as an offset from whichever of those two its waterway belongs to. Side waters — Spruce Creek, Rose Bay and Turnbull Bay — are followed as their own tributaries instead of being flattened onto the main river, so a spot up a creek is timed by the distance the tide really travels to reach it. Turnbull Bay is timed the way the water gets there — up the Halifax, into Spruce Creek, through Three Bridges and down the bay — not across from the Indian River. The Indian River North is now measured the whole way down — New Smyrna Beach, Packwood Place and Turtle Mound are all real gauges, so spots between the inlet and Turtle Mound are timed by interpolation rather than guesswork. South of Turtle Mound there is nothing to measure against for a long way, so once you get more than about five miles past it the app stops guessing: it shows raw Ponce Inlet times, tells you it has done so, and flags the forecast low confidence. Down there the water really does run hours behind the inlet and the wind moves it further, so read the conditions rather than the clock.

The tide stations are chips — the larger round shapes on the map — marked , and the wave buoy carries a chip of its own.

Waves flies to a National Data Buoy Center (NDBC) buoy pin and opens its live conditions: wave height, dominant and average wave period, mean wave direction, and water temperature, pulled straight from NOAA's National Data Buoy Center, each with its observation time. Needs internet to refresh, but no longer to be useful: the last reading is kept on the device, so if the fetch fails you still get the numbers with how old they are written on them — Last reading 3h ago. Three-hour-old figures still tell you whether it is building or laying down. When it can’t refresh it also says why, since the three causes are not the same problem: no internet (nothing to retry until you have signal), couldn’t reach NDBC (the relay, which goes down more often than the buoy — worth another try in a minute), or the station isn’t reporting (NDBC answered and sent nothing, so it is the buoy rather than your connection, and it will not clear up in a minute). Whichever it says, there is a Try again button under it, and the proxy-and-error detail is folded away under Details for the rare day it needs diagnosing. The buoy is 41070, 13.8 nm north-north-east of Ponce Inlet, off Daytona — measured from the compass rose, at 023° true. Its position is printed on the pin’s own popup in both forms: 29°17.340′N 80°48.180′W, the deg-and-decimal-minutes every other pin here uses and what you would key into the plotter, with the decimal degrees in brackets after it, (29.289 N 80.803 W), which is how NDBC’s own station listing writes it.

The buoy is a chip — one of the larger round shapes on the map — marked .

My Log opens your full catch history, listed by date caught, most recent first — not by the order you added them, so a catch you enter later, but that happened earlier, drops into place by its own date. Each catch also shows the moon phase for the moment it was caught — a moon icon plus % lit and whether it was waxing or waning — computed on-device from the same astronomy the Bite forecast uses, so it fills in automatically for every catch, old and new. Every catch card and spot popup carries EDIT and DELETE buttons, and one UNDO button sits at the top of the log — always there, even after you delete your last catch. It reverses your most recent change — an edit or a delete, on a catch or a spot, whichever came last — stepping back through up to your last 10 changes, one per tap. The same button sits above Your saved spots in the + Spot sheet; both work the identical history. Undone edits only last the session, but a deleted catch or spot is kept for 14 days (the last 10 deletions), so UNDO still brings it back after the app is closed or reloaded — the "Recently deleted" line under each UNDO button counts what's waiting.

On a phone, use Add to Home Screen to launch it like an app. Each person's catches and notes stay private on their own device. The My Log sheet has two exports. Full backup — wtf-full-backup-date.json — carries everything, photos included, along with the spots you added, your edits to built-in spots, and your drop labels; photos make it big enough that email will usually refuse it, so use Share and pick AirDrop or Save to Files. Log only — wtf-log-only-date.json — is the same data with the photos stripped out, small enough to email or text; catches restored from it have no photo, and there is no way to get those photos back from that file. Share hands either file straight to the iPhone share sheet — Mail, Messages, AirDrop — rather than putting it in Downloads. Import backup reads either one back in on a new copy or another device and adds only what this device hasn't seen; if it can't, it says exactly which check failed rather than shrugging.

Seasons opens the Season Guide — a month-by-month table for every species the app knows, for the Northeast zone (north of the NSB South Causeway). Each row carries its Size and Bag Limit for Atlantic waters off Volusia, an FWC ↗ link to FWC’s page for that fish, and black cells marking months closed to harvest (a season that turns over mid-month blacks out the whole month). Three buttons open the details, each closing again with CLOSE ✕: SIZE & BAG LIMITS for how to read the numbers and which zone they cover, POSSESSION for what you may have aboard, and REGULATION CHANGES for every limit that has moved, newest first. Limits refresh on their own whenever you open the app with a signal — no download — so Internet is required to update the app for the current FWC regulations. FWC and Fish Rules (fishrulesapp.com) are always the live word. Trust But Verify!

Reading the season month bars. Every colored bar row you see — in the Season Guide, in a pin’s popup, on a My Log card, or under Your saved spots — is a calendar: 12 cells, January on the left through December on the right. Brighter cells are the better months for that species; dim cells are the slow season. Only the Season Guide's bars add black cells for closed harvest months; the bars on popups, catch cards and saved spots show the bite alone. In popups, the letters above the bars mark the months. A catch shows a bar for every species on it, and a spot shows one for every fish you have named in its Details box.

Map zones. The guide also carries the zone key the whole map is colored by. Inshore is creeks, rivers, cuts, streams, flats, jetties, docks and ramps. Offshore is the natural reefs, the artificial sites and the wrecks, 3.5–39.1 sm out. Every catch and every spot is filed under one zone or the other — that is what the Inshore and Offshore map filter buttons switch, and what the + Catch and + Spot zone pills set.

Reef site coordinates are centroids computed from FWC's Artificial Reef Program deployment records for Volusia County (191 individual drops grouped into 16 sites, data as of Mar 6, 2026). Every county site leads with its number. Tap a reef pin and hit "Show drops" to see every individual deployment with its coordinates, listed closest-to-farthest from the inlet. Sites 4, 9, 10 & 11 sit 19.6–39.1 sm (17–34 nm) out and are outside the default view; pan/zoom to find them.

Compass puts a chart-style compass rose on the water just off the inlet mouth and gives you the run out to any offshore mark. Switch it on and only the rose appears. Hover a pin on a computer, or tap one on a phone, and a single dashed line runs from the rose out to that pin. Every leg is labelled the same way: the heading to steer and the run in statute miles, on one row centred on the line and running along it — 156°  4.3 sm. With a single pin up, the heading carries its reciprocal as well — 156°/336°  4.3 sm — read like any to/from pair: the first number is the course out, the second is the course home to the inlet, since with one pin the line out and the line home are the same track. On a route of several legs the reciprocal stays off — there it would be the way back along the route, not home, and the trip home is the route reversed. With one bearing on the row nothing can be confused with anything, so the words To and From are gone too. The gap between the heading and the run opens up as you zoom in and closes again as you zoom out, where every pixel of label crowds something. The line is cut away behind the text, so nothing is drawn through the numbers, and on a leg too short for both the heading stands alone. String a second leg on and the From comes off: a route is one-way, and its return is the route read backwards. The To stays on the leg out of the inlet, where there is a heading home to tell it apart from; on every leg after that the bearing stands on its own, since there is nothing to distinguish it from. In place of the word To the heading carries a small needle, the same solid needle the rose draws on its cardinal points, pointing the way you would travel; it flips end for end where the label has been turned to keep its digits upright, so it always points along the leg rather than back down it. Headings are magnetic, so they read the same as your chartplotter and your steering compass. Rather than hang an M off every number, the rose says it once for the whole overlay: MAGNETIC · VAR 7.3°W 2026 is printed beneath it, which is how a paper chart declares the variation on its own rose. Offshore popups say (magnetic) once beside their to/from figures, and a drop list carries one note at its head rather than an M on all nineteen rows. On a route of several legs the reciprocal is not printed — a second number on every line is clutter, and the run home is the route read backwards; the single-pin run is where the pair lives. The label slides itself along the line to wherever it won't be covered by the rose, the pin, or any other site's name tag (the site's popup and its drop list carry the distance as well, in both units, along with the reciprocal if you want it).

It works on offshore sites only — the county reef Sites, the wrecks and ledges, any offshore site you've added yourself, and your own logged catches out there. Inshore spots, launches, and inshore catches are left alone, since a bearing from the inlet is no use for a creek or a bridge. While the compass is switched on, tapping an offshore pin shows its bearing instead of opening its details — the popup would sit right on top of the line you asked for. Switch the compass off and pins open normally again.

Tap out a route. The rose gives you the run out from the inlet; tapping further marks strings the rest of the trip onto the end of it. Tap an offshore mark and you get the leg from the rose out to it. Tap a second and a leg is added from the first mark to the second — the inlet leg is not dropped, so the line reads rose → first ground → next ground and on for as many as you tap, each leg carrying its own heading and distance. Every mark on the route gets a ring, so the run reads as a chain of ringed grounds rather than a set of lines you have to trace to work out the order. Tapping any mark that is already on the route clears the whole route in one tap — a route is one thing you are planning, so it comes off in one piece rather than leg by leg. Tapping open water clears it too. Where a route gets busy the labels sort themselves out: each new leg looks for a clear stretch of its own line and steps around the labels already drawn. Any of the marks the compass covers can go on a route — reef Sites, wrecks, ledges, your own offshore sites and your offshore catches, in any order.

One caution worth knowing: the rose sits where a boater would actually pick up a heading, out past the inlet mouth, which is not the same point the app measures each site's nm-and-bearing figures from in its popup. For the three closest sites those two numbers can differ by 15–30°; further out they agree within a few degrees. The distance now printed on the line is measured from the same place the bearing is — the rose — so it too will read a little differently from the nm figure in the site's own popup, most noticeably on the closest sites. A site-to-site leg has no such problem: both ends are the marks themselves. All of it is a planning aid for getting the lay of the grounds in your head, not a substitute for your chartplotter. Every bearing the app prints is magnetic — the route legs and the to/from figures in the offshore popups and drop lists alike — declared once beneath the rose rather than on each number. The popups and drop lists still print both directions; only the lines on the map are one-way. Variation at Ponce Inlet is taken as 7.3° west (WMM, 2026), added to the true bearing the geometry gives, so nothing here disagrees with the compass in front of you. It drifts a little further west each year, so it is worth a re-check every few years. The one figure left in true degrees is the buoy's Mean Wave Direction, which is NOAA's own reading rather than anything this app worked out; its popup says so.

There is a third reference point in play, and it matters most for the county reefs. The nm and bearing printed in a county reef Site's own popup are FWC's published figures, carried straight across from the Artificial Reef Program's deployment records rather than calculated by this app — and FWC measures them from 29°04.500′N 80°55.500′W (29.0750, −80.9250), a point out in the inlet mouth channel. That is not the point this app uses for everything else. Its own offshore nm/bearing figures run from 29°04.902′N 80°56.202′W — inside the end of the north jetty, about 0.7 nm northwest of FWC's origin. The compass rose is further seaward again, at 29°04.653′N 80°54.385′W. Three origins strung along a mile of water, so three slightly different numbers for the same run, and that spread is most of why the closest sites disagree while the distant ones don't.

FWC's origin was not published with the records — it was recovered by fitting all 191 county drop coordinates against their stated distances. Every one of the 191 lands within 0.05 nm of that point, which is the rounding tolerance on a figure given to one decimal, so the fit is as exact as the source data allows. Your own natural-reef sites are a separate case: their distances were measured from close to the rose position, not from either inlet point.

Topo Satellite / Street Map (the label shows whichever view is currently active) switches between the satellite and street-map views.

Hi Res & ICW view. The map button cycles three ways: Topo Satellite, Hi Res & ICW, and Street Map. In Topo Satellite, zoomed out, the open sea is one flat ocean blue from about a mile off the beach — the same cut as the Hi Res & ICW photo, since the imagery's own offshore water is a patchwork of mismatched flight blocks that dominates at wide zooms — with Florida's state-waters limit (3 nautical miles on the Atlantic, 9 in the Gulf) drawn across the blue as a dashed line, and the coastal town names printed just off their beaches at the widest zooms, where the imagery's own labels would otherwise be cut off. A step closer in, where a printed name would only lose its tail to the blue, the blue steps back in a small window around the name so the map's own label shows whole. And from the 1-mile scale on in, the blue pulls back to the state-waters line itself, opening the whole strip of chart between the beach and the dashed line: the paddling-trail routes, the county boundary lines, the Intracoastal's course through the sounds and bays, and every island of the chains. Hi Res & ICW rides on its own hi-res aerial photo — one continuous image of the land and every inside water (the ICW, the lagoons, the bays), the sharpest view of the flats, bars and nearshore bottom, so the water you're picking a line over is shown at full detail (it has no printed place names, which the Topo Satellite keeps). Off the beach the photo gives way to the same single flat ocean blue as the Topo Satellite view — but here the blue follows the actual shoreline all the way around Florida, Atlantic and Gulf, with enough margin that the surf, the inlet jetties and the islands stay in the photo — and shades the federally maintained channels of Volusia County over it in cyan — the Intracoastal the whole way through the county, and the St Johns River along the county’s western boundary from Lake Monroe up past Lake George, so you can see the dredged cut itself rather than guessing it from the markers — useful for picking a line through the Halifax or down the Indian River, and for seeing how far off the channel a spot really sits. It is the channel area, not a centreline, and every stretch of it in Volusia County is authorised and maintained to 12 feet. It is stored on your device, so it draws with the signal off.

Channel markers. The Hi Res & ICW view also plots the 240 charted aids to navigation along those channels — 217 fixed daybeacons and 23 buoys — as small red and green dots, red for the marks on your starboard hand coming in from sea, green to port, and amber for the two or three preferred-channel junction marks. Tap a dot — or near enough to one, since a tap takes the closest mark within about a finger’s width — for its full charted name and, where it is lit, its light characteristic — Halifax River Light 47 · Fl G 4s. The name stays put until you tap another mark to move it or open water to clear it, and with a mouse hovering does the same thing. They come and go with the channel shading, since they belong to it.

The numbers start again on every waterway, which is worth knowing before you go looking for one. There are five marks numbered 47 in Volusia County alone — on the Halifax River, at New Smyrna Beach, in Mosquito Lagoon and elsewhere — so "marker 47" on its own does not identify a spot. That is why every dot carries its full name rather than just a number. Positions come from NOAA's electronic navigational charts (Harbour-band cells); the light characteristics are matched to each mark by position from the charts' separate light records. Same caution as the channel itself: aids get moved, go missing and change characteristic, so this is for planning, not for running an inlet at night.

The outlines come from the US Army Corps of Engineers' National Channel Framework — the Florida East survey published June 2020 — selected by the survey’s own county labelling. Treat it as paperwork, not as soundings. It shows where the channel is authorised to be, not where the water actually is now: shoaling moves the usable water around inside these outlines, and this coast gets plenty of it. Read your sounder and your chartplotter; use the shading to get the lay of the channel in your head, the same caution that applies to the compass rose.

Locate Me drops your GPS position on the map (tap again to remove it). The small red person figure on the Locate Me button signifies a MOB function.

MOB (man-overboard) function. Press and HOLD Locate Me for at least 1 second to activate — the pill floods red while you hold. The app drops a MOB mark at your position and starts guiding you back: a red banner at the top of the screen shows the bearing to steer (magnetic, read it against your compass), the distance (feet when you're close, miles when you're not), and a clock running since the press. A dashed red line runs from your boat to the mark — a red figure in a dashed ring — and the screen stays awake while it's up. The chart clears itself for the job: the species pills, the buttons (all but Locate Me) and every other pin leave the screen while MOB is active, and return when it's cleared. The mark takes the first fix available, immediately, then tightens itself if a sharper GPS fix lands within a few seconds; a boat under way covers a lot of water while a perfect fix is awaited, so fast-and-rough wins here. It survives a reload or a phone restart — the banner comes straight back. Tap the banner to see boat and mark together; CLEAR (it asks first) takes it down and keeps the mark in your spots as a record — a red pin named MOB with its date and time, filed under Inshore or Offshore by where it happened. To delete one later, tap its red pin and use Delete, or open + Spot and scroll to Your saved spots: MOB entries sit together alphabetically, each with EDIT ✎ and DELETE ✕ buttons — DELETE ✕ removes it. One thing to do at the dock, not on the water: the first time MOB (or Locate Me) is used, the phone asks permission to use your location — answer Allow While Using App now, so a real emergency press drops the mark instead of waiting behind a permission dialog. Two honest cautions: the mark is where the phone was when the button was pressed, not where the person went in, and a person in the water drifts from the mark with current and wind — the longer the clock runs, the wider the circle. This is an aid to memory, not a rescue device: the drill is still a spotter who never stops pointing, flotation in the water, and a VHF call.

Species Buttons

The colored diamonds down the left edge of the map — one for each of the 23 species the app knows.

The species buttons are the 23 colored diamonds down the left edge of the map — one per species the app knows.

The species buttons down the left side filter your catch log: tap one and the map shows only your catch diamonds for that species — the fishing-spot pins step aside until you switch it back off. A picked species stays visible at any zoom, and shows even if Catches is off. If you've never logged that fish, you'll get a note saying so.

They filter your catch log only, not the fishing spots, and only one species is picked at a time — tap the lit one again to clear it. Their labels follow the Labels map filter button, and the Eye takes the whole column off the chart along with the action buttons.

Map Filter Buttons

The row of buttons across the top of the map, under the header, are the map filter buttons — they decide which pins the chart is showing. Each carries its own total, and the totals count every built-in and user-added spot at any zoom level.

The map filter buttons are pills (hot-dog shapes) in the row across the top of the map, under the header — Catches, Inshore, Offshore, Launches and Labels. The number on each of the first four is a total count.

Shows and hides your catch diamonds — every fish in your log, colored by species. The number beside it is your total number of catches.

Catches within 100 ft of each other merge into one diamond with a count badge — tap it and every fish logged at that spot opens as a scrolling list of log cards, newest first, each with its own ✎ and ✕ button.

Your catches show on the map as small colored diamonds, one color per species; the fishing spots, sites and launches show as small colored pins. A diamond or pin carrying a number is more than one thing in the same place — tap it to read them all.

An on/off switch for the inshore fishing pins — the creeks, rivers, cuts, flats, jetties, docks and bridges. Turn it off and that whole zone leaves the chart; the number beside it is how many inshore spots there are.

Every waterway and island the Topo Satellite view names inside our water — from Tomoka Basin south to the Volusia County line — carries its own inshore pin, 63 of them: creeks, coves, bays, cuts, sloughs, flats, points, canals and islands, named exactly as the chart prints them. Names and positions come from the USGS Geographic Names Information System, the gazetteer the topo tiles label themselves from, so a pin sits where the map's own label sits, and searching a name you read off the chart finds it. Creek pins land at the creek's mouth, which is the point USGS files a stream under. Where a charted name and a spot name disagreed, the chart won: Tenmile Creek is one word, and the cut is Ponce de Leon Cut, spelled as its ICW daybeacons are. The Mosquito Lagoon waypoint, which had drifted 4½ miles west into the marsh, was put back under the name the map prints. The map stops at the county line: the Brevard end of the lagoon, the Haulover and Merritt Island are off it. The chart names two different Turnbull Creeks, so the southern one is pinned as Turnbull Creek Mosquito Lagoon W.

An on/off switch for the offshore pins — the county reef Sites, the natural reefs, the wrecks and ledges, and any offshore spot you added yourself. Turn it off and that whole zone leaves the chart; the number beside it is how many offshore sites there are.

An offshore pin carrying a number is a reef with more than one drop on it — the number is how many sites are at that named artificial or natural reef.

Offshore pins have a Show drops button that lists every individual deployment for the county reefs and for clustered natural reef sites — coordinates in degrees and decimal minutes, depth, distance, and bearing to/from the inlet — sorted closest to farthest from the inlet, and plots them on the map while the popup is open. Each drop pin is numbered to match its position in the list, so you can verify GPS numbers pin-by-pin. Each row is wider than the popup — swipe or scroll sideways within the list to bring the depth, distance, bearing, and any additional details into view. Tap any row to give that drop a name — the name then prints at the end of the row and is saved on this device; rows you have not named simply end at the bearing. If a popup covers the pins, drag it out of the way by its title area.

Shows and hides the boat ramp and kayak launch pins, independently of everything else, with its own total. Launches are left out of the + Catch location list on purpose — they are land points rather than places you fish.

Turns the name labels on or off for whatever pins are showing. Off means no labels, but the pins stay exactly where they were.

Search, Help & View Buttons

Five round cookies sit in the top-right corner of the header, in the order they are listed here, and a sixth — the map credits ⓘ — sits in the bottom-right corner of the map.

Search is a cookie — one of the round buttons in the top-right corner of the header.

Tap the 🔍 button next to Help and type a location name (e.g. "snook alley"), a launch (e.g. "swoop"), or a species (e.g. "pompano"). Results show matching location pins, every spot tagged for that species, and your own logged catches of it. Tap any result to fly to it on the map with its popup open — hidden pins are switched on automatically. Search also looks through this Help: type a topic (e.g. "tide station" or "offline") and matching Help sections are listed under their own heading — tap one to open Help at that section.

Help is a cookie — the round ? button in the top-right corner of the header.

Opens this help. The buttons on this page are the app's own buttons — tap one to read what it does, tap it again to close it. PRINT THIS HELP, below, prints the whole thing as plain text with every one of those writeups opened out, so you can read it away from the phone.

Search also looks through this help: type a topic into 🔍 and matching help sections are listed under their own heading.

Any popup that opens on the map — a spot, a catch, a reef with its drops showing — can be dragged anywhere on screen so it isn't covering the pins underneath. On a phone: press and hold anywhere on the popup that isn't a button, then slide your finger; the popup follows and stays put when you lift off. On a computer: click and hold anywhere on the popup that isn't a button or link, then drag. Buttons, links and the scrolling drops list still work normally, so you can drag from the popup's title or body text. The 3-Day Tide Forecast panel moves the same way — drag it by its title bar.

Don't need to hunt for a close button: tapping anywhere outside an open popup — elsewhere on the map — closes it, and tapping the dimmed background behind an open sheet (Log a Catch, Search, Bite, and the rest) closes that too.

Updates. Phones cache this app hard enough that a new build can hide behind an old copy for days. The app now checks quietly for a newer build — every time it opens, and when it comes back to the foreground (those paced to once every 10 minutes) — and if one is out, a small pill appears above the build stamp: UPDATE AVAILABLE — Tap to Reload. One tap brings the new build in; the ✕ puts it off until next time. No connection, no check — it never interrupts you on the water.

Themes is a cookie — one of the round buttons in the top-right corner of the header.

Tap 🎨 to pick a color theme — four dark options (Parrot Head, Green-Eyed Lady, Purple Haze, Tequila Sunrise) and Blue Suede Shoes and Brown Sugar, designed for reading in bright sun through polarized lenses. Saved on your device. A fresh copy of the app opens on Tequila Sunrise, the one that matches the icon and the opening screen; pick any other and it opens on yours from then on.

Text Size is a cookie — the round A button in the top-right corner of the header.

Tap A to set the reading text size (100%, 115% or 130%) for the panels and popups. The buttons follow along at half strength — at the 130% setting the map buttons, map filter buttons, species switches, the pins' name labels, and the count badges on the pins and catch diamonds print about 15% bigger, growing their pills a little to fit rather than wrapping. The size is saved on your device.

On a computer: if the whole app suddenly looks tiny, the browser has zoomed the page out (usually an accidental Ctrl+scroll or trackpad pinch while moving the map). Press Ctrl+0 — ⌘0 on a Mac — to reset it to 100%. The browser remembers the fix.

The Eye is a cookie — one of the round buttons in the top-right corner of the header.

Tap the Eye to clear the map furniture out of the way — it hides the whole column of buttons down the right, the species pills, and any tide gauge pins Tides has up, leaving the chart, your fishing pins and the map filter buttons. The gauges go hit area and all, so a hidden pin cannot be tapped by accident; a gauge popup left open closes on the way out. An open eye means they are showing; a closed eye means they are hidden, so the cookie always reads as the state of the map rather than as the action. Nothing is reset or unloaded: your filters, species switches and any compass route stay exactly as they were and reappear untouched. Like the theme and the text size, the setting is remembered on your device.

A popup opens clear of the controls on the map — the map pans itself so the whole window sits below the map filter buttons, inside the species column and the button stack, and above the scale and credits. Turn the Eye off and it uses the room the hidden buttons free up. Where a popup is simply too big for what's left — the Waves readings on a small phone — its top is what stays visible, since that is where its title and first readings are; drag it from there if you want to see the rest.

Map credits. The bottom-right corner carries a small ⓘ cookie. Tap it and the credits for whatever chart is currently drawn open above it — USGS, USDA NAIP and Sentinel-2/EOX on the satellite views, OpenStreetMap on the street map — and tapping it again, or tapping open water, puts them away. They used to sit on the map permanently, wrapped over two or three lines, and on a smaller phone the Satellite pill covered them. They have to be on the map rather than on a credits page — that is a condition of the licences the imagery comes under — but one tap behind an obvious control satisfies that, which is how every other mapping app does it. The Eye deliberately does not hide the ⓘ: a credit you can switch off is not a credit.

Tide Stations & Offline Maps

Two jobs worth doing at home, on wifi, before a trip.

You can add gauges of your own. Tap OPEN THE TIDE STATION TOOL below, and under Your Own Tide Stations, enter a name, a position, and how many minutes after the Ponce Inlet the high and low arrive — no measurements are needed. Saved stations act as real calibration points, so nearby pins pick up better timing straight away. A saved station gets a pin of its own, up whenever Tides is.

In the tool, fill in the name, the position and the two lag figures, then tap SAVE THIS TIDE STATION. It appears straight away as a pin of its own — up whenever Tides is — and every nearby forecast is re-timed against it. Each saved station is listed under the form with a DELETE ✕ beside it. Stations you save live on this device and travel in your backup files.

The app itself — all your spots, launches, reefs, catch log, notes, tide forecasts, search, and themes — works with no internet. The map imagery normally streams from map servers, but you can now download it for your fishing area so even the satellite view works with the signal off — do it once on wifi before hitting the water and the tiles are stored on your device. Add the app to your home screen for the most reliable offline launch.

Tap START THE DOWNLOAD below on wifi, before you leave, and the tiles for the area you pick are stored on this device. The app then draws that area with the signal off. It is a one-time job per area — run it again after you start fishing somewhere new.

Warning

Do not use this site for navigation. Although most of the GPS coordinates have been verified by scuba divers, assume site locations are approximations, because strong currents and high seas over time can shift and cover underwater sites. Likewise, exceptionally high winds and tidal fluctuations can shift the depth and configuration of inshore spots.

Disclaimer

Read this one before you take the app on the water.

The Compass overlay is for general reference only, not for setting a heading. A boater reads a bearing once clear of the inlet, not before, so the rose is anchored just offshore of the inlet mouth rather than at the same point each site's popup measures its nm/bearing figures from. For the closest sites — Lighthouse Point Reef, Site 14 Flagler Ave Reef, and Site 15 Sunglow Reef — that difference in reference point can swing the rose's bearing 15–30° from the number shown in the site's own popup; farther-out sites agree within a few degrees. Bear in mind those three popups are quoting FWC's figures, taken from 29°04.500′N 80°55.500′W in the inlet mouth channel — not this app's own reference inside the end of the north jetty, and not the rose. Close in, that choice of origin moves the bearing more than the run itself does. The distance printed on the line is measured from the rose as well, for the same reason and with the same caveat. A site-to-site leg sidesteps all three origins — it is measured between the two marks themselves. All of these figures are magnetic, 7.3° west of true — as the caption under the rose states; FWC published theirs in true degrees, so this app's rendering of a county reef's bearing is its own conversion of FWC's number, not FWC's wording.

No liability is assumed by the developer or owners of this app for any use of this app.

About

Where's The Fish?™
WTF Log

A fishing log and chart for the Halifax River, Ponce Inlet, Spruce Creek, Turnbull Bay and the grounds offshore of Volusia County — spots, launches, catches, tides, solunar bite times and buoy readings, kept on your own device.

Where's The Fish?™ and the redfish device are trademarks of Jan G. Neal.
© 2026 Jan G. Neal. All rights reserved.
Full credits, data sources and disclaimers are in Help.

Theme

Pick a color theme for the app. Your choice is saved on this device. Species and zone colors stay the same across themes so pins always read the same.

Add a Spot

Save your own fishing spot to the map. It's stored on this device and shows up like the built-in spots, including in the + Catch location list. Drop a pin or use your current location and name it. The app sets the type from where the pin landed, and you can override it.

Inshore
Offshore
Launch

Set a location and the app picks the type for you, or tap a pill to choose it yourself.

No location set yet.

Decimal, degrees-minutes, or full degrees/minutes/seconds all work — paste whatever your plotter or chart gives you.

Name the fish in your details — any species the app knows (redfish, trout, snook…) gets its season bars on the spot's pin and under Your saved spots below.

Check the type before you save. The app guesses it from the coordinates, and the guess is only as good as the coastline and channel lines it carries. Close to a bank, a jetty, or a ramp it can land on the wrong side. If the lit pill is wrong, tap the right one; your choice sticks and is what gets saved.

Your saved spots: 0.

Recently deleted: none.

Restoring brings back any built-in spots you edited or deleted. Your own added spots are not affected.

Create & Calibrate Tide Stations

Your Own Tide Stations

Add a gauge of your own — a dock, a bridge, anywhere you've timed the tide against the inlet. Saved stations become real calibration points: the forecast interpolates between them and the built-in gauges, so nearby pins get better timing too. Use a negative number for water that turns before the inlet.

No position set yet.

Leave Low blank and it copies the High value.

Your tide stations: 0.

FOR ADVANCED USERS ONLY

Calibrate Tide Lags

Turn a station's recorded water level into a real timing offset. The app already stores the inlet's NOAA high/low times, so this works offline once you paste the data. Pick a station, paste (or upload) a Stevens-Connect export, and tap Compute. If it looks solid, Save it — the tide panel will use it right away.

  1. Pick a station from the STATION dropdown menu below (e.g., Spruce Creek Park, Rose Bay Bridge, Dunlawton Ave, or Williams Point).
  2. Tap Upload file to upload a Stevens-Connect export.
  3. Tap Compute lag.
  4. If the data looks solid (app says is reliable), tap Save it and your tide app will use it right away. If you add the wrong data set to a station, simply follow these steps again to load the correct set to the station.
—

Needs a timestamp and a water-level column (extra columns like sigma/temp are fine — it finds the level column). Best export: Normalized interval or Raw readings in CSV at 6–15 min. Avoid hourly/daily aggregates (too coarse to time a high/low). NOAA CO-OPS / Ready formats work too, but are usually UTC — tick the box below. On the dashboard: station → Exports (or Trends) → 1w or a custom 1–2 week range. Two weeks gives the most trustworthy result.

The built-in station lags are locked. This tool measures and reports — it cannot write to them, on this device or any other. To change a built-in lag, edit TIDE_LAG_STATIONS in the source and redeploy, so every device gets the same number. The tide stations you added above are yours and stay fully editable.

Offline Map

Download the satellite map — USGS Imagery Topo over the land and Sentinel-2 imagery over the water — for the whole fishing area (Ponce Inlet, the Halifax and Indian Rivers, Mosquito Lagoon, and the offshore reefs). Do this once while you have wifi; afterward the map draws with the signal off. Tiles are stored on this device only.

Zoom 16 (closest) isn't offered for download — at well over a gigabyte it's too large to store reliably on a phone. The saved levels cover navigation and spot-finding; if you're offline and zoom in closer than the saved level, the imagery may go blank until you zoom back out or reconnect.

Do not use this site for navigation.
